units.translation: You, having come as a suppliant, are nevertheless pure and harmless to the house.
I have completed, I have brought to perfection
perfect in age; this is from animals
having completed: perfect. Properly of irrational animals, when it has shed all its teeth
to begin, to make a beginning
to begin, to make a beginning
Who began the battle, the Greeks or the others?
to extinguish, to quench
to extinguish, to quench
improperly, to dry up
κατέσβηκα [I have been dried up] I am dried up
in an interpolated verse, which the scholiast explains somehow as: "τὰ δάκρυα τῆς πατρίδος ποία παύσει τιμωρία [what punishment will stop the tears of the fatherland?]"
What justice will quench the source of my mother?
There is the sea; who will quench it?
The rushing fountains of tears have been dried up.
what punishment will stop the tears of the fatherland
I have been dried up
to rage against something with panting
to rage against something with panting
Like a horse panting against the reins, he waits.
to dig under and overturn, to raze
to dig under and overturn, to raze
having razed Troy
undermining, razing
undermining
razing, destruction
θανόντων κατασκαφάς [the burials of the dead] Sophocles says Ant. 920.
It seemed good to bury Eteocles with the dear burials of the earth.
For I will devise a tomb and burial for him.
having made destructions for the city
Alas, the destructions of the house!
the burials of the dead

covering, shelter

the covering of the corpse, the foot-entering shelter of the coffin

to rush upon, to fall upon

shady, shadowy

shaded with freshly plucked branches

to dash down, to destroy
and not without dispute, indeed, having been dashed down

to drip down, to shed in drops

establishment, institution
the arrangement of the choruses

to turn about, to overturn
passive
i.e. I have been compelled.
Where do you turn the end of your words?

now the overthrows of new ordinances

Phrynichus p. 433 ed. Lob. mentions it from Menander and severely criticizes it, not without reason, as Lobeck taught in his annotation: about which I have spoken in Thes. vol. 4 p. 1376.
But the word καταφαγᾶς [glutton] in Myrtilus the comic poet is utterly wicked (it is wrongly written καταφαγάς), even if Aeschylus (fr. 352) had used it first.
